title: SpecMPK: Efficient In-Process Isolation with Speculative and Secure Permission Update Instruction
problem: Memory Protection Keys (MPK) enable user-space access control for in-process isolation, but the permission update instruction (WRPKRU) is serialized, imposing significant performance overhead when applications require frequent domain switches to enforce isolation of critical data and pointers.
motivation: In-process isolation protects against memory safety vulnerabilities (buffer overflows, use-after-free) and speculative execution attacks, but the serialization cost of MPK permission updates makes it impractical for high-frequency domain-switching scenarios.
method: SpecMPK executes the memory permission update instruction (WRPKRU) speculatively—out-of-order, without waiting for earlier instructions to finish. The processor monitors all memory accesses that follow: if any try to access memory whose permissions were temporarily loosened by the speculative update, the processor blocks them from taking effect. These blocked accesses are allowed to proceed only once the permission update itself is guaranteed to happen (past the point where it could be undone). This prevents attackers from reading protected data through speculative execution while the processor gains speed by overlapping the permission update with useful work.
key_novelty: SpecMPK allows the memory permission update instruction (WRPKRU) to execute out-of-order speculatively while preventing speculative access to memory regions whose permissions were temporarily loosened, by blocking such accesses until the update is guaranteed to happen.
contributions: Analysis of WRPKRU serialization as the dominant performance bottleneck for MPK-based in-process isolation
SpecMPK microarchitecture: speculative permission update execution with transient-access blocking until non-squashable
12.21% average performance improvement for SPEC workloads requiring frequent domain switches vs serialized WRPKRU
Security argument that speculative execution attacks cannot exploit transiently upgraded permissions

limitations: Not discussed; evaluation limited to SPEC workloads; real-world application domain-switch frequency impact may vary.
